kurz: How combined options bet on a limited section of the price distribution at a price fixed in advance, instead of only on a direction.

bloecke.md:
A single option bought resembles insurance without an upper limit of cover. It is expensive, but its potential return is open-ended on the upside. With a single option sold, it is the other way round: the income is limited, and the risk hardly at all. Practically every combination of two or four legs, by contrast, corresponds to an insurance policy with an excess and a sum insured. You only pay for the section of the price distribution that you want to cover and sell the rest back to the market.

A spread is therefore a cheaper and more narrowly defined bet than a single option. You give up profit potential that you consider unlikely anyway and receive a premium for it immediately. In return, the result no longer depends only on the direction; it also depends on a range and a point in time.

All the calculations in this lesson are based on the same illustrative calculation: underlying at €100, remaining term three months, implied volatility 25%, interest rate 2%, no dividend. The premiums are calculated using Black-Scholes and rounded to the cent. A contract is for 100 units, and all figures are per share. For the euro amount per contract, they are multiplied by 100.

bloecke.titel: Option premiums in the model chain (per share, 3 months remaining)

bloecke.md:
## Vertical spreads with the same expiry and two strike prices

In a bull call spread, the call 100 is bought for 5.22 and the call 110 is sold for 1.80. The net outflow is 3.42, which is both the total investment and the maximum loss. The profit only grows up to a price of 110, because from there on every further euro of price gain is lost again on the call sold. The maximum profit is 10 minus 3.42, that is, 6.58.

The comparison with a single call bought is revealing. The single call 100 costs 5.22 and only makes a profit above 105.22. The spread is already in profit above 103.42, because it shifts the break-even point down by 1.80. This noticeably increases the probability of success. The price for this is giving up any profit above 110. An investor who considers a price rise to 106 likely and one to 130 unrealistic uses the spread to sell price opportunities that they do not expect anyway.

The bear put spread is the mirror image: long put 100 for 4.73, short put 90 for 1.22, net cost 3.51, maximum profit 6.49, break-even point at 96.49.

bloecke.formel:
Max. profit + max. loss = strike width
Break-even = reference strike ± net premium
bloecke.erklaerung: For every vertical spread with equal quantities, maximum profit and maximum loss together add up to exactly the distance between the two strike prices. This allows you to check any entry in the broker's order screen quickly for plausibility. If the equation does not work out, something has been entered incorrectly.
variablen: difference between the two strikes, here 10
the strike that the price must reach first

bloecke.titel: Bull call spread 100/110 against the underlying (illustrative calculation, per share)
bloecke.unter: The profit starts earlier than with the single call and ends at 110; giving up profits above 110 pays for the lower break-even point.

bloecke.md:
Beginners consider credit spreads superior because money comes in immediately. The calculation refutes this. A bear put spread 90/100 costs 4.73 − 1.22 = 3.51 (debit). The bear call spread with the same strike prices brings in 11.67 − 5.22 = 6.45 (credit) and risks 10 − 6.45 = 3.55.

Both positions gain when prices fall. They have the same strike width, and profit and loss are capped at the same price points. With the rounded premiums, the maximum loss differs by 3.55 − 3.51 = 0.04, and unrounded by 0.0499, that is, around 5 cents. This corresponds to the interest on €10 over three months: 10 × (1 − e^(−0.02 × 0.25)) = 0.05. Put-call parity does not allow any other difference. Anyone who chooses a credit spread because it means “collecting premium” gains only the interest difference and a different pattern of entries in the account.

## Bets on movement instead of direction

In a long straddle, a call and a put with the same strike price are bought, here for 5.22 + 4.73 = 9.95. A profit only arises at prices below 90.05 or above 109.95. The maximum loss of 9.95 occurs if the price is exactly 100 on the expiry date. With the straddle, you are therefore betting that the move will be bigger than the one already priced in. With 25% volatility and three months, the range of fluctuation expected by the market (one standard deviation) is 100 × 0.25 × √0.25 = 12.5%. The break-even points therefore lie within one standard deviation. That is why a straddle quite often ends with a narrow profit, yet still loses on average, because in the long run implied volatility is above the volatility realised later.

The long strangle 95/105 costs only 2.59 + 3.17 = 5.76. In return, it only makes a profit at a price below 89.24 or above 110.76. Between 95 and 105, both legs expire worthless. With the strangle, the total loss therefore occurs across a whole price range and not just at a single point.

For at-the-money options, the approximation `straddle price ≈ 0.8 × S × σ × √T` applies. In the example chain, this gives 0.8 × 100 × 0.25 × 0.5 = 10.0, and the straddle costs 9.95. Conversely, the straddle price divided by 0.8 gives the move that the market assumes as one standard deviation until expiry. Before a scheduled event, this is the quickest way to check whether your own expectation is greater than the move already paid for.

## Butterfly and iron condor with four legs

In a long call butterfly 95/100/105, one call each at 95 and 105 is bought and two calls at 100 are sold. This costs 8.07 − 2 × 5.22 + 3.17 = 0.80, and no more than that can be lost. The maximum profit of 5 − 0.80 = 4.20 is reached exactly at 100, and the break-even points are 95.80 and 104.20. The reward-to-risk ratio of 5.25 to 1 looks very favourable. However, the maximum profit is only reached at a single price, and the position hardly reacts until shortly before expiry.

The iron condor is based on the same expectation but covers a wider price range: short put 90 (+1.22), long put 85 (−0.48), short call 110 (+1.80), long call 115 (−0.96). This gives a net credit of 1.58, a wing width of 5, a maximum loss of 5 − 1.58 = 3.42 and break-even points at 88.42 and 111.58. As long as the price stays between 90 and 110, all four legs expire worthless and the credit is kept.

bloecke.titel: Iron condor 85/90/110/115, net credit 1.58 (illustrative calculation, per share)
bloecke.unter: Between 90 and 110 there is a broad, flat profit zone; in return, the possible loss is more than twice as large as the best possible profit.

bloecke.md: With the iron condor, a possible profit of 1.58 is set against a possible loss of 3.42. Looking, for simplicity, only at the two extreme cases, the position has to deliver the full profit in 3.42 / 5 = 68.4% of all cases for the result to be zero, before fees. The fact that this condor expires with a profit in around 65% of cases in the model therefore follows from the design of the payoff profile and is no evidence of a good strategy. The overall result is decided by the rarer cases in which the price runs through one of the wings.

## Calendar spread across two maturities

All the combinations so far have a common expiry date. In a calendar spread, a short-dated option is sold and a long-dated option with the same strike price is bought, here a short call 100 with one month to expiry (2.96) and a long call 100 with three months (5.22). The net cost is 2.26. There is no payoff diagram in the usual sense for this, because the long leg still has time value when the short leg expires. The value of the remaining position therefore has to be calculated and cannot simply be read off.

The calendar spread can work because time value decreases with the square root of the remaining term and not linearly. An option with one month remaining therefore loses significantly more time value per day than the same option with three months. This difference is what the calendar spread earns. In exchange, the position carries vega risk. The long leg reacts more strongly to implied volatility than the short one, so the position loses when implied volatility falls. If the price stays at 100 and implied volatility falls from 25% to 20%, the profit falls from 1.97 to 1.16 per share. That is €81 per contract, even though the price has not moved.

bloecke.titel: Result of the calendar spread 100 (1M/3M) at expiry of the short leg
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with implied volatility constant at 25% for both maturities; in calm markets, the volatility of the short leg is usually lower, which makes the spread more expensive, and under stress or before scheduled events it is often higher.

bloecke.titel: Seven basic combinations compared (model chain, per share)

bloecke.unter: The axes show the direction of the price and the development of implied volatility; investors who only take the direction into account systematically choose a combination from the wrong half.

felder.text: Debit strategies buy volatility and direction at the same time. The spread caps the profit but moves the break-even point closer to the price.
A rare combination, because volatility usually rises when prices fall. Debit spreads are cheapest here.
A credit strategy that sells time value above the price and also profits without any price movement.
A credit strategy below the price. The iron condor extends it to both sides of the price.

bloecke.md:
## Margin at the broker

With options bought, you pay the premium and nothing else. No more than the premium can be lost, so no collateral is required. It is different with options sold. An uncovered short put 100 risks up to €10,000 per contract. The margin for it is based on the simulated loss in a stress scenario and not on the premium.

Eurex Clearing calculates margin on a portfolio basis using the **Prisma** model. What is assessed is what can happen to the portfolio as a whole in a stress scenario, and not each position individually. For a spread with a bought wing, the collateral is therefore close to the maximum loss of the position, so for the iron condor above roughly 5 minus the credit, times 100 units, times the number of contracts. Eurex deliberately does not state fixed euro amounts. The rates are recalculated daily on a risk basis and rise when volatility rises. Additional capital is therefore tied up precisely when a position is showing a loss. Positions in an account that is regularly run with a margin utilisation of 80% are therefore forcibly closed out in the first real period of stress.

The broker only recognises the legs as a unit under two conditions. They must be held in the same account, and the long leg must run at least as long as the short leg. With a calendar spread whose sold leg runs longer than the bought leg, an uncovered short option position remains after the bought leg expires. The margin is therefore calculated from the outset as if the position were uncovered.

bloecke.titel: Combination orders instead of separate orders
bloecke.md: If the long call is bought first and the short call is sold an hour later, the risk in the meantime is completely different. In addition, the full bid-ask spread is incurred twice, and the second leg may not be executed at all. Combination orders are executed as one order at a net premium or not at all. This also applies to closing. If only the protective leg of a spread is closed out, the remaining position is uncovered from that moment on, and the margin rises accordingly.

## Taxation of the individual legs

The flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) covers each individual transaction on its own; a strategy as a whole is not considered for tax purposes. Under Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG (Income Tax Act), option writer's premiums received are income at the time they are received. The premium for a later closing transaction is taken into account as negative income at the time of payment. The bought leg, on the other hand, is treated as a derivative transaction (Termingeschäft) under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG. Under Section 20(4) sentence 5 EStG, the gain is the cash settlement less the expenses directly connected with it. The premium of one leg is not an expense of the other, so at the level of the individual settlement nothing is offset within the spread.

Since the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024, the former cap of €20,000 a year on offsetting losses from derivative transactions (Section 20(6) sentence 5 EStG, old version) has been abolished without replacement. It no longer applies in any open cases (Section 52(28) EStG). With multi-leg strategies, the winning leg and the losing leg could previously diverge for tax purposes. Since the abolition, their results can be offset normally again. The general loss pot (allgemeiner Verlusttopf) continues to apply. Losses from capital assets may only be offset against other capital income or carried forward to subsequent years; offsetting against wages or rents is ruled out (Section 20(6) sentences 1 to 3 EStG). The separate share loss pot (Aktientopf) under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG does not affect options.

bloecke.titel: Positions over the turn of the year
bloecke.md: A credit spread opened in December and not closed until January is spread over two assessment periods. The premium received is taxed in the old year, while the closing premium paid only takes effect as negative income in the new year. With a losing trade, tax therefore first becomes due on a profit that never existed in economic terms. Investors who hold open option-writing positions over the turn of the year should plan for this. If they have securities accounts at several banks, they should also apply by 15 December for the loss certificate (Verlustbescheinigung) under Section 43a(3) sentences 4 and 5 EStG, because otherwise gains at one bank and losses at the other remain unoffset. This does not replace tax advice; legal position as of September 2026.

The **diagonal spread** combines different strike prices with different maturities. It behaves like a calendar spread with an additional view on direction and is correspondingly harder to manage, because vega, theta and delta act at the same time.

The **ratio spread** is more dangerous. In it, more options are sold than bought, for example a long call 100 against two short calls 110. It looks like a butterfly with a missing wing. In the example chain, it costs 5.22 − 2 × 1.80 = 1.62 (debit); with the calls sold closer to the price, it often even brings in a credit. Above 110, however, one leg is uncovered, and the loss potential is open again. What counts for the risk is therefore the number of uncovered contracts; the size of the premium does not change this. If the line in the payoff chart does not run out horizontally at the right or left edge, the result is unlimited in that direction.

mitnehmen: With a spread, you sell the part of the price distribution that you do not expect anyway and thus move the break-even point closer to the current price; in return, the profit is capped.
For every vertical spread, maximum profit and maximum loss together add up to the strike width. The debit and credit variants with the same strikes differ only by the interest on this width.
A high reward-to-risk ratio goes hand in hand with a low probability of success and vice versa; the iron condor in the example chain needs a hit rate of 68.4% to break even.
The price of an at-the-money straddle is approximately 0.8 × S × σ × √T and therefore shows which move the market has already priced in.
Margin is not a down payment. It is collateral that is recalculated daily and rises precisely when the position is showing a loss.

For tax purposes, each leg counts separately, and the €20,000 limit for derivative transactions has been abolished without replacement by the Annual Tax Act 2024. Option-writing positions that are open over the turn of the year remain unfavourable.

begriffe.text: Combination of a bought and a sold option of the same type with the same expiry date and different strike prices. Maximum profit and maximum loss always add up to the difference between the strike prices.
Balance of the premiums paid and received across all legs. A debit means a cash outflow on opening and is also the maximum loss. A credit means an inflow and is the maximum profit.

Position with four legs, namely a short put spread below and a short call spread above the price. It earns the credit as long as the price stays within the middle band. The maximum loss is the wing width minus the credit.
Sale of a short-dated option and purchase of a long-dated option with the same strike price. The profit comes from the faster time decay of the shorter maturity; the position is net long vega.
A single order with which all legs of a strategy are executed at a specified net premium or not at all. It prevents risks between the individual executions and double costs from the bid-ask spread.
